n: David uses courtroom and battlefield language at once: be my lawyer against those who accuse me, and my warrior against those who attack me.

f.g: Argue my case, as an advocate in court.

n: He pictures God arming himself like a soldier and rising to defend him.

f.g: A small round shield (or a large body shield); paired with “shield” for full protection.

n: David asks God to block the pursuers’ road with a spear — and, most of all, to reassure his soul: “I am your salvation.”

f.w: say unto my soul, I am thy salvation
f.g: What David wants most is a personal word of assurance from God.

n: He prays that his would-be killers will be frustrated and forced to retreat in disgrace.
May they be blown away like chaff — the light husks separated from grain in the wind — with the angel of the Lord driving them.

f.g: The dry husks blown away when grain is winnowed.

n: He asks that their road become dark and slick as they flee, with God’s angel in pursuit.
His enemies had no reason to attack him, yet they dug a hidden pit and spread a net to catch him, like hunters trapping an animal.
David asks that their own trap catch them by surprise. The Psalms often teach that evil boomerangs on those who plot it.

f.w: let his net that he hath hid catch himself

n: When God rescues him, David’s whole soul will rejoice in that salvation.
Even his bones — his whole being — will cry out: no one is like the Lord, who rescues the weak from the strong and the poor from those who rob them.

f.w: LORD, who is like unto thee

n: Lying witnesses accused him of crimes he knew nothing about — a situation Jesus would also face.
They repaid his kindness with harm, leaving him feeling bereaved and desolate.

f.w: to the spoiling of my soul
f.g: Leaving my soul bereft, like one who has lost a child.

n: David contrasts his behavior: when they were ill, he wore mourning clothes and fasted for them. His prayer “returned into his bosom” — he prayed with head bowed to his chest, or the blessing came back to him.

f.g: Coarse cloth worn in mourning or humility.

f.w: my prayer returned into mine own bosom
f.g: Either “I prayed with head bowed on my chest,” or “my prayer came back unanswered for them, but blessed me.”

n: He grieved for them like a brother, like a son mourning his mother. That is how deeply he cared.
Yet when David stumbled, they celebrated and ganged up on him — even lowlifes and strangers joined in, tearing at him nonstop.

f.g: Outcasts, lowly people; possibly “smiters” or slanderers.

n: Like freeloading mockers at a feast, they ground their teeth at him in hatred.

f.w: gnashed upon me with their teeth

n: “How long will you just watch?” David pleads with God to rescue his precious life from these lion-like enemies.

f.g: My only one — my precious, solitary life.

n: He vows to praise God publicly in the great congregation once he is rescued.
He asks that those who hate him for no reason won’t smirk and wink at his downfall.

f.g: A gesture of malicious scheming or gloating.

n: They don’t speak peace; they cook up lies against peaceful, quiet people who mind their own business.

f.w: them that are quiet in the land

n: They open their mouths wide in mockery: “Aha! We saw it with our own eyes!” — gloating over his troubles.
David answers: but you, Lord, have seen it too. Don’t stay silent or distant.
“Wake up and take my case!” David speaks boldly, as if God were asleep — honest language that the Psalms allow in prayer.
He asks God to judge by God’s own justice, so his enemies won’t get to celebrate.
Don’t let them say, “Just what we wanted — we swallowed him whole!”
May those who delight in his harm be wrapped in shame instead, like wearing a garment of disgrace.
In contrast, let David’s supporters shout for joy and keep saying, “The Lord is great — he delights in his servant’s well-being.”
The psalm ends with a vow: David’s tongue will talk about God’s justice and praise all day long.
